name: Minocycline foam
lead: Topical minocycline foam is a prescription formulation of the tetracycline antibiotic minocycline, designed to deliver the drug to the skin while keeping systemic exposure low. People use it to clear inflamed acne lesions (4% foam, brand Amzeeq) and the bumps and pustules of papulopustular rosacea (1.5% foam, brand Zilxi), which helps the face look calmer, clearer and more even.[1][2][8][9]

The 4% foam (developed as FMX101) was tested in moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris and the 1.5% foam (FMX103) in moderate-to-severe papulopustular rosacea. Phase 3 randomised, vehicle-controlled trials ran for 12 weeks in both conditions and reported greater reductions in inflammatory lesion counts than vehicle foam.[1][2][3][8] A pharmacokinetic study found that plasma exposure after topical use was several hundred times lower than after an oral minocycline tablet.[4]

The US FDA approved the 4% foam for acne in 2019 and the 1.5% foam for rosacea in 2020.[8][9] Both are prescription products; no looksmaxxing-community discussion of them was found, and they appear in this wiki because of their use on acne and rosacea.

paras: The 4% foam is approved in the US for inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate-to-severe acne in people aged 9 and older.[5] Its high lipid content is described as helping the drug move through sebum into affected follicles, and in vitro work reported that the favourable resistance profile of oral minocycline against Cutibacterium acnes was maintained with the topical form.[5]

FMX103 1.5% was developed to bring minocycline's anti-inflammatory benefit to rosacea while limiting the systemic side effects associated with oral tetracyclines.[2] The Medical Letter reviewed the foam under its brand name for rosacea.[9]

In a phase 1 crossover study of 30 people with moderate-to-severe acne, a single oral extended-release minocycline tablet was followed ten days later by 21 days of once-daily 4% foam at a 4-gram maximal-use dose. Plasma levels after topical use were very low (geometric mean Cmax about 1.1 to 1.5 ng/mL), steady state was reached by day 6, there was no accumulation, and overall exposure was 730 to 765 times lower than with the oral tablet. No serious or treatment-related adverse events were reported.[4]
A phase 2 randomised, vehicle-controlled study of the foam in acne was published in 2016, preceding the phase 3 programme.[6]

Two identical phase 3 studies (n=961 in total; 466 and 495) randomised participants 2:1 to once-daily 4% foam or vehicle for 12 weeks. The co-primary endpoints were change in inflammatory lesion count and Investigator Global Assessment success (clear or almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement). Both studies reported significantly larger reductions in inflammatory lesions with the foam, and the foam also reduced non-inflammatory lesions.[1] A third 12-week, 1:1 randomised phase 3 study in 1,488 participants reported greater reductions in inflammatory lesions and better IGA success than vehicle, noting that mild acne was not characterised.[3]

A 2025 multicentre phase 3 study in China randomised 372 people 2:1 and found a greater 12-week reduction in inflammatory lesion count with the foam than vehicle (about -21.0 versus -12.3), with acceptable tolerability.[10] A review reported that extension data indicated continued effectiveness for up to 52 weeks, that most patients rated the product satisfactory or highly satisfactory, and that cutaneous adverse events were uncommon.[5]

A phase 2 study evaluated FMX103 in facial papulopustular rosacea before the phase 3 programme.[11] Two 12-week, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials (registered enrolments of roughly 750 each) then compared 1.5% foam with vehicle. In both, the foam produced a significantly larger reduction in inflammatory lesion count (for example -17.57 versus -15.65 in one and -18.54 versus -14.88 in the other) and maintained a favourable safety profile. The authors noted that results should be examined in real-world settings.[2][7]
Earlier foam formulations of minocycline were also tested in a phase 2 study in children with impetigo.[12]

In the trials the foam was generally well tolerated; most adverse events and all serious adverse events in the acne programme were considered unrelated to treatment, and cutaneous reactions were uncommon.[5] Because systemic absorption is low, the foam is intended to avoid many effects seen with oral minocycline, but full prescribing information and a clinician's advice apply.[4][5]

The foam is marketed as Amzeeq (acne) and Zilxi (rosacea) in the US and is regarded as part of a trend toward topical antibiotic delivery that limits systemic exposure.[5][9][13] As a prescription drug it is not part of the looksmaxxing forum canon, where people discussing acne more often name oral antibiotics, retinoids or isotretinoin.

timeline.event: Phase 2 results of topical minocycline foam in acne published.[6]
Pharmacokinetic study shows far lower systemic exposure than oral minocycline.[4]
Phase 3 acne results for FMX101 4% published; US approval for acne.[1][8]
Phase 3 rosacea results for FMX103 1.5% published; US approval for rosacea.[2][9]
Phase 3 study in Chinese participants with acne published.[10]

card.summary: Prescription minocycline foam trialled in Phase 3 for acne (4%) and rosacea (1.5%).
card.note: Prescription antibiotic; not an over-the-counter product.

quick.overview:
Topical minocycline foam is a prescription antibiotic foam for acne (4%) and papulopustular rosacea (1.5%).

Both strengths were tested in multiple randomized, vehicle-controlled Phase 3 trials.
quick.mechanism: It delivers the tetracycline antibiotic minocycline directly to the skin, aiming to limit systemic exposure compared with the oral drug.
quick.risks: Specific adverse-event figures are in the trial reports. It is a prescription antibiotic; oral minocycline is a distinct, systemic product.

chain: Minocycline reduces inflammatory lesions of acne or rosacea
Fewer red bumps and pustules, clearer-looking skin
angle.text: Applied once daily by prescription to the face in the trials, the foam is aimed at reducing the inflamed papules and pustules that dominate how acne and rosacea look. In 12-week trials participants had larger drops in inflammatory lesions than vehicle foam.
